notes: Ruling slot 1 holds the Nacionalista Party of Marcos (MD 2000 had NP in slot 20; its MD sprite PHI_Nat_Populism moves with it). Slot 2 Liberal Party is the real opposition, not a coalition partner; no party shared power with the NP on 1 Jan 1970. CPP kept in slot 4 as in MD (slot 19 has no popularity); the old pro-Soviet PKP-1930 goes to slot 6 as the Eastern-bloc orthodox hardliners; Kabataang Makabayan fills the Maoist slot 19. Philippine Constabulary in slot 0 as Marcos' pro-US internal security instrument, separate from the AFP in 22. Shia slots use small Iranian student circles in Manila.

0.name: Philippine Constabulary
0.text:
The Philippine Constabulary is the national gendarmerie, created under American rule in 1901 and today one of the four major services of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. It polices the provinces, hunts bandits and smugglers, and carries the counter-insurgency war against the Huk remnants and the new Maoist guerrillas of Central Luzon. President Marcos has made it his preferred instrument of internal order and keeps its command in trusted hands.

Its officers, trained alongside American advisers and steeped in anti-Huk doctrine, see the country's crisis as a security problem: they favour emergency powers, curbs on radical students and a firm alliance with Washington. With detachments in every province, the Constabulary is the force on which any move toward authoritarian rule would depend.

1.name: Partido Nacionalista
1.text:
The Nacionalista Party, founded in 1907 and the oldest party in the country, governs the Republic. In November 1969 Ferdinand Marcos became the first president to win a second term, defeating the Liberal Sergio Osmeña Jr. in a campaign remembered for its lavish spending, while the party also holds the vice-presidency under Fernando Lopez and the Senate presidency under Gil Puyat.

Like its rival, the party is a coalition of provincial clans and patronage networks rather than a programme. It stands for close ties with the United States, private enterprise, roads and public works, and rice self-sufficiency. The costly campaign has left a balance-of-payments crisis, and the student movement is turning against Malacañang. Its leverage lies in presidential patronage and control of Congress.

2.name: Partido Liberal ng Pilipinas
2.text:
The Liberal Party, formed in 1946 by Manuel Roxas as a breakaway from the Nacionalistas, is the main opposition. Its candidate Sergio Osmeña Jr. was crushed in the 1969 presidential election, but the party remains strong in the Senate, where Gerardo Roxas, Benigno Aquino Jr. and Jovito Salonga lead the attacks on Marcos's spending, the military and the creeping concentration of power.

Ideologically the Liberals differ little from the Nacionalistas: both are alliances of landed and provincial families, pro-American and committed to private enterprise. The party's younger senators, however, increasingly speak the language of reform, civil liberties and land redistribution, and Aquino has made himself the most prominent critic of a possible Marcos dictatorship.

3.name: Christian Social Movement
3.text:
The Christian Social Movement was launched in 1968 by Raul Manglapus, former foreign secretary and 1965 presidential candidate, together with Catholic intellectuals, lay activists and Christian trade unionists. It is a small opposition formation preparing for the Constitutional Convention due in 1971, which it sees as the chance to rebuild the Republic on new foundations.

Inspired by Catholic social teaching and European Christian democracy, it calls for genuine land reform, workers' participation in industry, an end to the rule of political clans and a parliamentary system. It is firmly anti-communist and Western-oriented, but critical of American economic privileges. Its strength lies in Catholic schools, the Federation of Free Workers and Manila's reform-minded middle class.

4.name: Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas
4.text:
The Communist Party of the Philippines was re-established on 26 December 1968 in Pangasinan by Jose Maria Sison and young cadres who broke with the old Lava leadership of the PKP. Underground and illegal, it counts only a few hundred members, mostly students and activists from Kabataang Makabayan, but its programme already proclaims a protracted people's war.

The party defines the Philippines as semi-colonial and semi-feudal, ruled by American imperialism, landlords and comprador capitalists. Following Mao Zedong Thought, it looks to Beijing rather than Moscow and seeks to surround the cities from the countryside. Its leverage lies in the radicalised campuses of Manila and in its armed wing, the New People's Army, founded in Tarlac in 1969.

5.name: Bagong Hukbong Bayan
5.text:
The New People's Army was founded on 29 March 1969 in Capas, Tarlac, as the armed wing of the re-established Communist Party. Its commander, Bernabe Buscayno, known as Kumander Dante, brought over a band of former Huk fighters; at the start of 1970 the army has a few dozen rifles and operates among the tenant farmers of Tarlac and neighbouring provinces.

The NPA wages protracted people's war on the Maoist model: small units, rent reduction, punishment of abusive landlords and Constabulary informers, and patient political work in the barrios. It rejects elections and parliamentary reform as illusions and is hostile to the American bases. Its leverage is the deep agrarian grievance of Central Luzon.

6.name: Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas-1930
6.text:
The Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas, founded in 1930, is the old communist party that led the Hukbalahap against the Japanese and the Huk rebellion of 1946–1954. Outlawed since 1957, it has been shattered by arrests: its general secretary Jesus Lava has been in prison since 1964, and the 1968 breakaway of Jose Maria Sison's Maoists took most of its youth.

The remaining leadership follows the Soviet line, condemns the Maoists' armed adventurism as premature and prefers legal mass work through peasant unions, labour federations and nationalist fronts. It hopes for legalisation and for Manila to open relations with Moscow and Eastern Europe. Its residual strength lies among veteran cadres in Pampanga and Tarlac and in the trade unions.

7.name: Lapiang Malaya
7.text:
Lapiang Malaya is the millenarian movement of Valentin de los Santos, an aged mystic who promised his followers true independence and the downfall of corrupt rulers. On 21 May 1967 several hundred of its members, armed with bolos and amulets, marched on Malacañang and were cut down by the Constabulary on Taft Avenue in Pasay; dozens died, and de los Santos himself died weeks later in the National Mental Hospital.

The survivors, scattered across the Tagalog provinces, preach an end to American influence, the expulsion of foreign bases and capital, and rule by a righteous national leader in place of the elected oligarchy. Its leverage is the deep anti-elite resentment of the rural poor, which the massacre has only sharpened.

8.name: Anjoman-e Eslami
8.text:
The Anjoman-e Eslami is a small Islamic association of Iranian students enrolled at Manila universities, among the young Iranians who choose the Philippines for affordable English-language degrees in medicine, engineering and agriculture. It meets for Friday prayers and Muharram gatherings and keeps contact with similar student associations in Europe and the United States.

Its members follow the reformist Shia thought of Mehdi Bazargan and the Liberation Movement of Iran, combining faith with science, constitutionalism and opposition to the Shah's dictatorship and American tutelage. Politically insignificant in Philippine terms, it is the only Shia political voice in the islands and a link between Filipino Muslim students and the currents of Islamic modernism in Iran.

9.name: Hey'at-e Hosseini
9.text:
The Hey'at-e Hosseini is a mourning circle of devout Iranian students and traders in Manila who gather for the rites of Muharram and the recitation of the sufferings of Imam Hussein. Its core members are followers of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled since 1964 and now teaching in Najaf, and they circulate his sermons and letters in mimeographed pamphlets.

They reject the Shah as a usurper and American puppet and hold that the ulama must lead the community and the state. In the Philippines they seek converts among Muslim students from Mindanao and preach Islamic revolution as the answer to both capitalism and communism. Tiny and watched by Iranian intelligence, the circle has no leverage beyond its zeal.

10.name: Ansar El Islam
10.text:
Ansar El Islam is the leading Muslim religious association of Lanao, founded in Marawi by Ahmad Domocao Alonto, former senator and the most respected Maranao statesman of his generation. It runs madrasas, sends students to al-Azhar and Saudi Arabia, helps organise the hajj and represents Philippine Muslims before Middle Eastern governments and the Muslim World League.

It stands for orthodox Sunni practice, Arabic education and the dignity of Muslim institutions within the Republic, preferring negotiation with Manila to rebellion. Close to the sultans and datus of Lanao and to Saudi and Egyptian patrons, it seeks recognition of Islamic law in personal matters and state support for Muslim schools. Its leverage lies in its religious authority among the Maranao.

11.name: Top 90
11.text:
Top 90 is the name given to the first batch of about ninety young Moros secretly trained in guerrilla warfare on Pangkor Island in Malaysia in 1969, with the backing of Sabah's chief minister Tun Mustapha. Recruited after the Jabidah massacre of March 1968, they include the University of the Philippines lecturer Nur Misuari alongside other students and sons of datus.

The trainees reject the traditional Muslim politicians as collaborators of Manila and see armed struggle as the only answer to Christian settler encroachment and military abuses. They speak of a free Bangsamoro nation and of jihad against Philippine colonialism, drawing on Islamic solidarity from Malaysia and the Arab world. Their leverage is a secret cadre waiting for a spark in Mindanao.

12.name: Muslim Independence Movement
12.text:
The Muslim Independence Movement was proclaimed on 1 May 1968 by Datu Udtog Matalam, former governor of Cotabato, in the wake of the Jabidah massacre, in which Muslim recruits were killed by their army trainers on Corregidor. Its manifesto calls for an independent Islamic republic of Mindanao, Sulu and Palawan.

The movement is led by traditional datus and educated Muslim notables rather than clerics, but it speaks the language of Islamic solidarity and of protection against Christian land-grabbing and settler migration. It seeks Muslim self-government, Islamic law and education, and the sympathy of Malaysia and the Arab world. Its leverage rests on the alarm of Cotabato's Muslim population and on Manila's fear of secession.

13.name: Mga Teknokrata
13.text:
Mga Teknokrata is the circle of American-trained economists, engineers and managers whom Ferdinand Marcos has drawn into government since 1966. Its rising figure is Cesar Virata, former dean of business administration at the University of the Philippines and chairman of the Board of Investments, flanked by economists from the UP School of Economics and planners of the Presidential Economic Staff.

The technocrats want a strong executive insulated from Congress and the old clans, export-oriented industrialisation, tax reform and planning, and they see the balance-of-payments crisis as proof that patronage politics cannot govern a modern economy. They are not party men and owe loyalty to the President alone. Their leverage lies in their indispensability to creditors such as the IMF and World Bank.

14.name: Iglesia ni Cristo
14.text:
The Iglesia ni Cristo is the indigenous Christian church founded in 1914 by Felix Manalo, who died in 1963 and was succeeded as Executive Minister by his son Eraño Manalo. Disciplined and fast-growing, with imposing chapels in towns across Luzon, it claims hundreds of thousands of members and is courted by every presidential and senatorial candidate.

The church takes no part in party politics as such but votes as a bloc on the instruction of its leadership, rewarding friends and punishing enemies, and Marcos has cultivated it with care. It is socially conservative, anti-communist and hostile to Catholic dominance of public life, valuing order, discipline and church autonomy over any ideology. Its leverage lies entirely in its unified vote.

15.name: Sugar Bloc
15.text:
The Sugar Bloc is the alliance of planters and mill owners of Negros, Iloilo, Pampanga and Batangas who have dominated Philippine politics since the American era. Its most powerful family is the Lopez clan of Iloilo: Vice President Fernando Lopez and his brother Eugenio Lopez, whose empire includes the Manila Electric Company, the ABS-CBN network and the Manila Chronicle.

The bloc lives on the preferential American sugar quota and therefore defends close economic ties with Washington, cheap credit, low land taxes and the hacienda system against land reform. It funds candidates of both parties and expects favours in return. Its leverage is money and media, though Marcos is beginning to see the Lopez power as a rival to his own.

16.name: Philippine Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Philippine Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1903, is the oldest business association in the country and speaks for Filipino import and export houses, traders, bankers and retailers. Its leaders sit on government advisory boards and maintain close links with the American and Chinese chambers of commerce in Manila.

Unlike the protectionist Philippine Chamber of Industries, it favours free trade, the decontrol of foreign exchange, a floating peso and openness to foreign capital, and it welcomes stabilisation measures agreed with the International Monetary Fund. It distrusts nationalist restrictions on business and a swelling state sector. Its base is the commercial class of Manila, Cebu and Iloilo, and its leverage lies in its ties to banks, creditors and the Central Bank.

17.name: Bantay Gubat
17.text:
Bantay Gubat is a loose network of biologists, foresters, mountaineers and missionaries alarmed at the destruction of the Philippine rainforest by the logging boom of the 1960s. Its best-known voice is the zoologist Dioscoro Rabor, who has spent decades documenting the wildlife of Mindanao and the Visayas and warns that the monkey-eating eagle faces extinction.

The network calls for an end to reckless timber concessions, reforestation, protected national parks and respect for the lands of the upland tribes. It has no mass following and no party, and its arguments run against powerful logging families allied with both major parties. Its leverage lies in scientific prestige, the press and the support of foreign conservation bodies.

18.name: Federation of Free Farmers
18.text:
The Federation of Free Farmers was founded in 1953 by the lawyer Jeremias Montemayor and young Catholic activists to organise tenants and smallholders as a democratic alternative to the communist-led Huk movement. Still led by Montemayor, it has grown into one of the largest peasant organisations in the country, active in Central Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.

The federation demands genuine land reform, enforcement of the 1963 Agricultural Land Reform Code, fair rents, cooperatives and rural credit, and it organises rallies and legal campaigns against abusive landlords. It rejects both the landed oligarchy and armed revolution, looking to Catholic social teaching rather than Moscow or Beijing. Its leverage lies in its numbers and its standing with the Church.

19.name: Kabataang Makabayan
19.text:
Kabataang Makabayan was founded on 30 November 1964 by Jose Maria Sison and student activists from the University of the Philippines. Legal but under constant surveillance, it has become the largest radical youth organisation in the country, with chapters in universities, high schools, factories and barrios, and in 1968 its core followed Sison into the new Maoist party.

The organisation preaches national democracy: an end to American imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat capitalism, the removal of US bases and the abolition of parity rights. It looks to Mao's China as its model and sees itself as the vanguard of a coming revolution. Its leverage is the street: KM can fill Manila with demonstrators and feed recruits to the guerrillas.

20.name: Pilipino Muna
20.text:
Pilipino Muna gathers the politicians, small Filipino merchants and provincial notables who rally behind the slogan of former president Carlos P. Garcia: Filipino First. Garcia, a Nacionalista elder from Bohol, launched the policy in 1958 to reserve the economy for Filipino citizens against American and Chinese business, and he remains its symbol as the country prepares for the Constitutional Convention.

Its programme demands an end to American parity rights when the Laurel–Langley Agreement expires in 1974, strict enforcement of the retail and rice trade nationalisation laws, curbs on Chinese merchants and preferences for Filipino entrepreneurs. It is anti-communist but mistrustful of Washington. Its leverage lies in resentment of foreign economic dominance among the middle class and provincial voters.

21.name: Monkees
21.text:
The Monkees are armed anti-communist gangs active in Tarlac and Pampanga since the late 1960s, recruited from local toughs, former Huk informers and discharged soldiers and protected by elements of the Constabulary and the army. Named after an American pop group, they hunt suspected Huks and the young fighters of the New People's Army, and Senator Benigno Aquino Jr. has accused them of murders in his home province.

The Monkees have no programme beyond the extermination of communists and anyone who shelters them. They serve landlords, local politicians and military intelligence, and their violence drives new recruits to the rebels. Their leverage lies in fear and in the impunity granted by their patrons in uniform.

22.name: Sandatahang Lakas ng Pilipinas
22.text:
The Armed Forces of the Philippines, led since 1968 by General Manuel Yan as Chief of Staff, comprise the Army, Navy, Air Force and Constabulary. Trained and equipped under the 1947 Military Assistance Agreement with the United States, the officer corps upholds a tradition of civilian supremacy, though President Marcos, himself a decorated veteran, has steadily promoted loyal officers, many of them from his native Ilocos.

The military is deeply anti-communist and bound to the American alliance, the bases at Clark and Subic and the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization. Officers increasingly view the communist revival in Luzon and the Muslim unrest in Mindanao as threats demanding more power and resources. Its leverage is the monopoly of organised force.

23.name: Kasultanan sin Sug
23.text:
The Royal House of Sulu is the dynasty of the Sultanate of Sulu, which once ruled the Sulu archipelago and North Borneo. Its reigning head is Sultan Mohammad Esmail Kiram I, on the throne since 1950, recognised by the Republic as a traditional and religious leader but without political power. The heirs' claim to Sabah, revived by President Macapagal in 1962, poisons relations with Malaysia.

The house stands for Tausug identity, Islamic tradition and the restoration of its historic rights, including compensation or sovereignty over North Borneo. It cooperates with Manila when that serves the Sabah claim but resents Christian settlement and the neglect of Sulu. Its leverage lies in its legitimacy among the Tausug and the diplomatic value of its claim.
